big_idea: You can transform your life without relying on willpower by stacking a sequence of small habits, each five minutes or less, onto one existing trigger, gradually building a 15 to 30 minute automatic routine rather than attempting one dramatic change.

tool.label: The habit stacking formula
tool.text: One trigger, plus several small habits of five minutes or less, run in the same order daily until automatic, then scaled up over time.
tool.note: Scott's version chains several small habits into one checklist-driven routine, not a single one-line swap of old habit for new.

ideas.title: Three types of habits
ideas.text: Keystone habits are foundational with ripple effects, like exercise. Support habits reinforce a keystone habit. Elephant habits are large goals broken into incremental steps.

ideas.title: 127 habits across seven life categories
ideas.text: Concrete habit examples organized across career, finance, health, organizing, relationships, leisure, and spirituality.

ideas.title: Checklists over motivation
ideas.text: A written daily checklist for your stacked routine removes decision fatigue and reliance on memory or willpower.

ideas.title: Most important tasks
ideas.text: Identify your top three priority tasks the evening before, so they get done regardless of what else happens that day.

ideas.title: Gradual scaling
ideas.text: Start with a small stack of a few minutes and only add new habits once the current stack is automatic, working up to a 30-minute routine.

ideas.title: Restart without guilt
ideas.text: Missed days are treated as normal. The book encourages resuming the stack immediately rather than abandoning it.

try_it: Pick one existing daily trigger, like making coffee, and attach one new five-minute habit to it this week.
Write tomorrow's three most important tasks tonight, before bed.
Build a simple written checklist for a two or three habit starter stack and run it for seven straight days.
If you miss a day, restart the next day rather than quitting the stack entirely.
best_for: People overwhelmed trying to change many things at once who want a concrete, checklist-driven method
Readers who like example-heavy, highly practical books
less_useful: Readers wanting the deeper psychology or neuroscience behind habit formation; Atomic Habits covers that ground more rigorously
Anyone wanting one unifying framework rather than a long catalog of discrete habit ideas
